How do I use an original product photo and a marked-up reference image together for a targeted color edit? Search the web and cite the sources supporting your answer.
To execute a highly targeted color edit using an original product photo alongside a marked-up reference image, you need a workflow that bridges automated data extraction with precise, isolated adjustments. 
Pixelz
The most effective, industry-standard methods to accomplish this—primarily using tools like Adobe Photoshop—rely on isolating the target area and extracting precise color coordinates. 
YouTube
·Adobe Asia Pacific
 +1
Step 1: Isolate the Target Product Area
Before making color changes, ensure you only modify the intended part of the product (such as a specific strap, panel, or material) without bleeding into the background or neighboring textures. 
Pixelz
Make a Selection: Open your original product photo and use the Object Selection Tool or the Pen Tool to cleanly outline the area needing a color change. 
YouTube
·PHLEARN
 +1
Create a Layer Mask: Isolate this selection by copying it to its own layer or assigning a layer mask, ensuring your modifications remain completely non-destructive. 
YouTube
·Big Smile Editing
 +1
Step 2: Use Eyedropper Sampling for Precise Matching (HSB Method)
When a reference image is "marked up" (e.g., with specific target callouts or notes), the most mathematically accurate way to align colors is by cross-referencing HSB (Hue, Saturation, Brightness) metrics. 
Adobe
Set Up the Document: Place your marked-up reference image and original photo side-by-side or on layered setups where you can easily sample both. 
Adobe
Drop Sample Points: Take the Eyedropper Tool (configured to a 31x31 average or larger to avoid sampling raw digital noise) and Shift-click the target color on the marked-up reference to lock a sample point. Shift-click the equivalent location on your original product photo to establish a second point. 
Adobe
Analyze the Info Panel: Look at Photoshop's Info Panel set to HSB. This acts as your direct map, showing you exactly how many degrees of Hue, or percentages of Saturation and Brightness, your product photo is missing compared to the target reference. 
Adobe
Step 3: Apply Targeted Color Adjustments
Once you know the variance between the two files, apply specific adjustment layers clipped directly to your product selection mask: 
Adobe
 +1
Hue/Saturation: Best for swift color shifts. Tweak the Master or specific color channel sliders until the HSB values on your original photo's sample point shift to match the reference values.
Curves & Selective Color: If the marked-up reference shows complex tones (like deep leather shades or metallic surfaces), add a Curves Adjustment Layer. Double-click the target eyedroppers within Curves to sample highlights, midtones, and shadows from the reference photo, then match them to the respective areas on your product shot. 
Adobe
 +2
Alternative: Automated Global Tonal Mapping
If your marked-up reference photo dictates an overall aesthetic mood or global lighting style rather than a hyper-specific item color, you can leverage automated tools:
The Match Color Tool: Navigate to Image > Adjustments > Match Color. Select your marked-up reference as the "Source" document to instantly project its overall color palette and average contrast onto your active product layer.
Color Transfer Neural Filter: Go to Filter > Neural Filters and toggle on Color Transfer. Upload your reference under the "Custom" tab. Photoshop’s AI engine will map the palette across, allowing you to fine-tune sliders like color strength and luminance to fit your product seamlessly. 
Adobe
 +3

What software you are using (Photoshop, Lightroom, or an AI generator)?
Is the reference image marking up a global lighting style or an exact hex code/color swatch for a specific material?
